true_answer: We also sometimes say that “if and only if” statements have two directions: a forward direction ( P → Q ) and a backwards direction ( P ← Q , which is really just sloppy notation for Q → P ). Let’s think a little about which part is which. Is P → Q the “if” part or the “only if” part? Consider an example. Example 0.2.7 Suppose it is true that I sing if and only if I’m in the shower. We know this means both that if I sing, then I’m in the shower, and also the converse, that if I’m in the shower, then I sing.
